items.impact: The seed identifies its version, canonical status, owning schema, and registry source of truth, preventing projections from becoming independent authority.

evidence.exact_quote: "Provider config files, MCP projections, model-native tool declarations, coding-agent bridge files, and GUI settings rows are projections of these registry rows.",

"Projection examples serialize capability refs, health refs, egress policy refs, and credential refs only; they never serialize raw API keys, OAuth tokens, passwords, cookies, headers, or local machine paths.",
"Seeded provider capability claims cite packet/receipt provenance and keep health_state=unknown until an explicit live health/projection sync records current provider evidence."

items.impact: Projection authority, secret non-serialization, and the distinction between seeded claims and live evidence are directly constrained.
items.statement: The negative constraints make downstream files projections, forbid raw-secret and local-path serialization, and require live evidence before health can cease being unknown.
items.title: Projection and secret boundaries are explicit

items.impact: Rows provide machine-readable capability, rank, egress, and bounded-fanout inputs for a router or projection consumer.
items.statement: The registry rows encode per-operation support, enablement, health, caching, fallback rank, robots posture, SSRF policy, and provider-level egress limits.
items.title: Provider rows expose routing and egress metadata

items.impact: Implementations can disagree on legal transitions, stale-write handling, failure precedence, rollback, and what evidence authorizes a state change.
items.statement: Multiple independent state fields are seeded, but this excerpt gives no legal transition graph, transition authority, atomic update rule, stale-write policy, recovery path, or falsifiable transition oracle.
items.title: Registry state transitions and recovery are undefined

items.impact: A router cannot deterministically decide eligibility, rank ties, degradation, retry order, or offline behavior from these rows alone.
items.statement: Fallback ranks and health values are present, but selection precedence, tie-breaking, exclusion of unknown or unconfigured providers, retry budgets, and network-loss behavior are not specified.
items.title: Fallback routing semantics are not executable

items.impact: Stored web content may cross users, retain sensitive material, resist deletion, or be poisoned without a defined key, scope, invalidation, purge, and redaction-before-write contract.
items.statement: Caching is enabled with TTLs, but cache keying, tenant and credential isolation, sensitive-content classification, invalidation, deletion, poisoning resistance, capacity limits, and redaction timing are absent.
items.title: Cache privacy and deletion lifecycle are unspecified

items.impact: A GUI projection could present unknown health as healthy, conflate unconfigured with disabled, or expose hard-coded English without accessible status semantics.
items.statement: Rows provide display names and raw state tokens but no localized label key, accessible status wording, state-to-GUI mapping, stale-health warning, or user-facing reason contract.
items.title: GUI status truth, accessibility, and localization are open

items.impact: Consumers can distinguish native, composed, and partial behavior and, for Google-compatible search, select capability-specific egress policy.

items.impact: The same data can produce different provider choices and failover paths across implementations, especially during health uncertainty or network loss.
items.statement: Numeric ranks are present, but the excerpt does not define whether lower wins, how operation-specific ties are resolved, or how health, configuration, cost, and offline status alter precedence.
items.title: Fallback ranks lack a deterministic precedence contract

items.impact: The mixed provider-native and PM-composed Google-compatible row does not have to force all capabilities through one egress boundary.
items.statement: Google-compatible search explicitly maps provider-native search and PM-composed read or research operations to different egress policies.
items.title: Capability-specific egress override is explicit for Google

items.impact: Credential failure, provider outage, expired evidence, and partial capability recovery have no defined error classification, backoff, quarantine, operator action, or rollback behavior.
items.statement: Credential references and health references exist, but the seed does not define validation, expiration, timeout, retry, circuit-breaker, quarantine, or recovery semantics.
items.title: Credential and health failure recovery is absent

items.impact: Per-call limits alone do not prevent aggregate fanout amplification, races, quota exhaustion, or noisy-neighbor behavior across concurrent jobs.
items.statement: Rows bound local fanout and depth, but no global concurrency, queue, rate, quota, cancellation, accounting, or overload-observability contract is present.
items.title: Local limits do not define aggregate scale behavior

items.impact: Consumers can distinguish direct API, model-native, and coding-plan adapter families rather than treating all providers as MCP servers.

items.impact: PM is not implicitly authorized to rewrite model-native provider configuration or take custody of externally managed secrets.

items.title: MCP consumer projection examples are concrete

items.impact: A boolean assertion cannot prove generated files exclude secrets, unsafe paths, headers, or stale credential material, nor define remediation after a failed scan.
items.statement: Examples assert no secret serialization but provide no generator output schema, scanning oracle, provenance receipt, failure response, or evidence freshness requirement for that assertion.

items.impact: The registry can drive MCP consumers, PM-native direct API consumers, and a server bridge without treating their integration mechanism as identical.

items.statement: Consumer-specific provider lists differ, but the excerpt gives no eligibility predicate, exclusion rationale, required-consumer completeness rule, or authority for changing the matrix.
items.title: Consumer provider selection is unexplained

items.impact: A heterogeneous bridge may accidentally normalize distinct provider credential owners into one handling rule, creating custody and lifecycle ambiguity.
items.statement: Each coding-agent row provides one secret_policy for its entire heterogeneous provider list, with no per-provider override, credential-owner mapping, rotation responsibility, or revocation propagation contract.
items.title: Consumer rows collapse per-provider secret authority

items.impact: Runtime or template upgrades can change provider compatibility without a version gate, downgrade path, deprecation window, or golden projection oracle.
items.statement: The coding-agent projection examples have no per-row version, minimum runtime version, template version, migration state, rollback rule, or executable compatibility fixture.
items.title: Coding projection compatibility and migration are unversioned

segments.summary: The seed establishes registry authority, projection and secret constraints, and detailed provider metadata, but leaves routing, state transitions, cache lifecycle, and GUI state semantics under-specified.
Firecrawl, DuckDuckGo, and Google-compatible rows capture provider differences and a useful egress override, while deterministic routing, recovery, and aggregate scaling remain undefined.

The registry covers direct, model-native, and coding-plan adapters plus concrete MCP examples, but projection reference cardinality, drift recovery, and executable secret-safety verification are unresolved.
The coding-agent matrix names major consumers and projection kinds and the JSON closes cleanly, but provider eligibility, per-provider secret authority, and versioned migration contracts are absent.
